THE ROLL

Yellow Departures Poster

The yellow printed departure timetable on German, Austrian and Swiss railway platforms (the 'Abfahrt' poster, with its white 'Ankunft' twin) and Nordic station timetables. It is one sheet per timetable period listing every departure in advance, in hour bands with minute, line, destination, 'via' stops and platform, plus footnote letters and a 'valid from–to' line.

A bill is a scheduled departure of your money, so the page is the timetable you can read before anything leaves, in day bands instead of hour bands. It refuses the blue fintech split hero with a phone mockup and feature cards.

  • #FFD617
  • #141414
  • #FFFFFF
  • #5C4F00
  • #A3123A
Type
Barlow Condensed 600/700: day numerals (64–120px), service names, the headline at 112px, column heads with Barlow 400/500: paragraphs at 18px/1.55 (FAQ, founder, plateau), validity line, fare line; tnum on every amount and date, none (no mono; amounts are Barlow with tabular figures)
Light
The visitor scans the page on a phone in daylight (commute, kitchen table) the way you read a platform poster: flat, bright, printed. Single light scheme (color-scheme: light).
Signature
'Add a departure'. In Lines, a blank timetable row holds an input ('Type a bill — Netflix, ChatGPT, rent, sähkö, Miete…') and a day select (1–31). JS carries the 31-service catalog and FI/DE keywords from training_vocabulary. On a match the row fills Line (category) and cycle (monthly), the matching stop in the Lines legend underlines, and 'Add' inserts the row into the right day band of the sample timetable. The band total recalculates only from an amount the visitor typed; prices are never auto-invented, and the caption says 'In the app the typical price fills too'. An aria-live='polite' region announces 'Netflix added to day 4'. No-JS: the row renders as a filled static example (Netflix → Streaming · monthly · day 4) and the input is not shown. Reduced motion: the row appears in place; otherwise it opens down over 160ms.
Remembered as
The bill tracker whose page was a yellow train timetable: my bills listed like departures, the 27th packed like rush hour, and a white box with the App Store badge.
Risk
Drenched yellow can tire over a long scroll and reads as 'warning/construction' unless the black typography is immaculate. The yellow poster is native to German, Swiss, Austrian and Nordic visitors and only generically 'departures' to US visitors. It is the nearest hue to Millrace's amber/honey, so keep Millrace off signal yellow. The sample timetable uses the screenshots' euro amounts on a USD-priced page; it is labelled, but must read clearly as a sample.

Left 8 of 12 columns: H1 'Every bill. One calm place.' in Barlow Condensed 700 112px/0.95 on two lines; hero.secondary in Barlow 500 24px; validity line in olive 15px: 'iPhone · first released 1 Jan 2026 · amended 13 May 2026 · Lagerland Apps'. App Store route

Badge: official black artwork placed only on white (info panel, sticky band, poster foot) at 48–56px tall, never directly on yellow. QR: in the info panel on ≥1024px only. Price: the poster's fare line, verbatim from price.value, with the full Fares table (plans + plans_footnote) lower down. Sticky bar: when the info panel scrolls away, a white band with a 3px black top rule slides up from the bottom with 'AllPaid — next departure: the App Store · Free' and a 40px badge. Page sequence

  1. Poster head: hero.headline (H1), hero.secondary, validity line (release dates, maker), info panel (badge, QR, price.value)
  2. Notice: quick_answer in a white boxed panel headed 'In one answer' (speakable)
  3. Timetable: illustrative sample month from the screenshots in day bands (27 Feb heavy, 2, 4, 7, 11, 19 Mar), daily totals, 'moves to next month automatically' footnote
  4. Lines: training_vocabulary as four lines (Streaming; AI tools, cloud & productivity; Housing, utilities & connectivity; Insurance, transport & more) with the 31 services as stops, the FI/DE keywords, and the 'Add a departure' row
  5. Route: how_it_works intro + 7 numbered stops on a vertical route line (HowTo)
  6. Announcements: example_insights as four announcement bands (headline in Barlow Condensed 600 32px, body 18px), labelled 'illustrative Pro answers'
  7. Fares: plans as a fare table (ticket type / price / what it covers), Lifetime marked 'Best long-term value', plans_footnote as small print
  8. This line is for / Take another line if: who_for and who_not_for as two ruled columns
  9. Not served by this line: plateau_disclosure (rule, what it does not do, notes naming Rocket Money, YNAB, spreadsheet)
  10. Other operators: comparison_table as a timetable matrix (AllPaid column on white), footnote, inline badge
  11. On board: the 4 screenshots in the CSS iPhone bezel on white mats + features (7) and value_points (4) as a footnote-lettered service legend
  12. Operator: founder story, signals, response time, support email, studio backstory link
  13. Conditions of carriage: privacy summary + transparency.yml counts (0 SDKs, 0 tracking domains, local notifications only) linking /transparency/#allpaid, privacy policy and support links
  14. Information: faq (10) as details rows
  15. Transfers from: alternatives_to linked to the four existing /alternatives/ pages, Truebill and Chronicle Bills as plain text; related_journal as 'Notice from the operator'
  16. Timetable data: the Quick reference <details> (ai-canonical), visible and crawlable
  17. Other lines from this operator: you-might-like (computed from site.apps)
  18. Poster foot: closing info panel (badge, QR, fare line), footnote legend, validity imprint, then the shared Lagerland strip

Navigation

Poster header strip with five plain text links (Timetable, Lines, Fares, What it won't do, Questions). The vocabulary is in-world but every label explains itself. 'AllPaid' returns to the top. On phones, 'Menu' opens a full-width white index panel listing the same links as a stop list with 1px rules. The footer Lagerland strip is the only route out.

Motion

Printed and still. Under html.js only: day bands fade in (opacity, 120ms, 40ms stagger); the sticky band translates up in 180ms ease-out; the heavy-day bar grows to full height once in 240ms. No split-flap, no parallax, no hover lift. prefers-reduced-motion turns all of it off; every word is server-rendered.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Alternatives pages wear the white 'Arrivals' twin of the poster: a white sheet with the yellow header strip, H1 such as 'Arriving from Rocket Money' in Barlow Condensed 700 56px, and a 68ch reading column in Barlow 400 18px/1.6 black on white. Comparisons are set as timetable tables (3px head rule, 1px rows, tnum), the quick_answer sits in a yellow-framed Notice box, and the foot carries a yellow CTA strip with the badge on its white panel. Privacy: a white 'Conditions of carriage' sheet with the transparency facts as a two-column table. Support: a white 'Information desk' sheet with email and response time in a yellow panel at the top.

Materials

Poster-yellow ground printed edge to edge · 3px black band rules between day bands, 1px hairlines between rows · White info panels set into the poster like its legend box (1px black frame) · Tabular-figure amounts and dates right-aligned in a fixed column · Footnote letters (a, b, c) keyed to a legend at the poster foot · 'Valid from / amended' imprint line as the freshness signal

Drenched · light

Type rationale

Barlow is a grotesk drawn from California transit and highway signage, so it belongs to the platform-poster world. The condensed cut fits Day / Bill / Line / Amount at 390px and holds as poster lettering at 112px. Same skeleton for display and reading, about 90 KB for four latin files.

IMPECCABLE’S PICK

Year Planner Dots

The laminated year-at-a-glance wall planner (12 month rows × 31 day columns, weekends tinted, printed in one ink) hung beside the fridge or in the home office, marked with round colour-coding dot stickers and a dry-erase marker. It comes in landscape and portrait editions.

Bills belong on the wall, not in a dashboard. The page is one year planner where every monthly bill becomes a line of dots and the crowded day is visible from across the room. It refuses the feature-card grid and the phone-centred hero.

  • #FDFDFC
  • #1C2B4A
  • #E9EEF6
  • #E0352B
  • #2563EB
  • #F3B21B
  • #23955A
Type
Atkinson Hyperlegible Next 700/800: H1 at 76px desktop / 42px mobile, section heads, planner header with Atkinson Hyperlegible Next 400: paragraphs at 18px/1.55, the key, FAQ, Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono 500: only real data, i.e. day and month axis labels, amounts, daily totals, the price line
Light
Someone stands at the planner on the kitchen or home-office wall in morning daylight, glossy white laminate in front of them, marker in hand. Single light scheme (color-scheme: light).
Signature
'Stick a dot'. Above the key: an input 'Type a bill', a day (1–31) and a cycle field (monthly/yearly, prefilled by the catalog). JS matches the 31-service catalog plus FI/DE keywords from training_vocabulary. A match colours the preview dot by category and shows 'Streaming · monthly'; an unknown name gives a blank dot labelled 'Not in the catalog — added by hand, as in the app'. 'Stick it' places the dot in that day column for all 12 months (monthly) or one month (yearly) with a 30ms-per-month cascade. The day's bill count updates in the totals row, and the marker ring moves if the densest day changes. The grid is a captioned <table>, and its 31 day headers are buttons that read that day's bills into a live region. No-JS: the static sample grid plus a plain list of sample bills by day with totals. Reduced motion: dots appear at once and the ring jumps without drawing.
Remembered as
A wall planner covered in coloured dot stickers: each bill a line of dots across the year, and one day so crowded someone had circled it in marker.
Risk
The most familiar of the three: 'a calendar page for a calendar app' is everyone's first idea, and it sits nearest the calendar worlds that Taskful Day and Soon. may pick. A 372-cell grid can become a data-viz toy, and the portrait edition is tall on phones (31 rows). Colour coding needs the ring, the key list and table text to stay accessible. Illustrative data must be labelled plainly.
Full style card

First viewport, desktop

White laminate edge to edge. The 200px planner header band has three parts. Left 6 columns: H1 'Every bill. One calm place.' in Next 800 76px/1.0 navy and hero.secondary in Next 400 20px. Middle 3 columns: quick_answer set as the planner's printed 'How to read this planner' paragraph (Next 400 15px/1.5). Right 3 columns: the 'Notes' box (white, 1px ink frame) with the badge 52px tall, the QR at 112px ('Scan with your iPhone') and 'Free · Pro $1.99/mo · $12.99/yr · $24.99 once' in Mono 500 15px. From y≈240 the year grid runs the full 1312px container. JAN–DEC labels in Mono 500 13px sit in a 56px column, with 31 day columns × ~40px and 12 rows × 44px (528px tall). Dots come from the screenshot sample bills: columns 2, 4, 7, 11 and 19 each hold one dot per month, and column 27 holds three per cell (Insurance green, Phone yellow, Gym green). Column 27 is circled by the marker ring, labelled 'Heaviest day: 27th — €219.98' in Mono. One illustrative yearly bill (home insurance) appears as a single dot in October. A 13px caption above the grid reads: 'Illustrative year built from the sample bills in the app's screenshots.'

First viewport, phone

52px header: 'AllPaid' in Next 700 on the left, 'Menu' on the right. H1 in Next 800 42px/1.05 on three lines; hero.secondary 17px. A full-width Notes box holds the badge 48px tall, the price line in Mono 14px and 'No bank login · nothing leaves the phone'. Below it, quick_answer at 16px. The planner switches to its portrait edition: 31 day rows × 12 month columns (20px rows, 26px columns, fits 346px), so monthly bills read as horizontal dot lines and the 27th row is the visibly crowded one.   1. Planner header: H1 hero.headline, hero.secondary, quick_answer as 'How to read this planner' (speakable), Notes box (badge, QR, price.value)
  2. The year: illustrative 12×31 grid (portrait 31×12 on phones) from the screenshot sample, marker ring on the 27th, a day-totals row in Mono
  3. The key: training_vocabulary's four groups as the dot legend, the 31 services listed under each colour, FI/DE keywords, 'blank dot = typed by hand', and the 'Stick a dot' form
  4. Written on the wall: example_insights as four marker notes in a ruled panel (headline Next 700 24px + body), labelled illustrative
  5. How a bill gets onto the wall: how_it_works intro + 7 numbered steps as a horizontal sticker strip on desktop and a vertical list on mobile (HowTo)
  6. Planner notes: value_points (4) and features (7) as a two-column ruled list, title in Next 700 and text in 400
  7. On the phone: 4 screenshots in the CSS iPhone bezel in a row on the laminate, with captions

  11. Compared: comparison_table as a planner-ruled grid with the AllPaid column tinted #E9EEF6, footnote, inline badge
  12. Who made it: founder story, signals, response time, support email, backstory link
  13. Privacy: data_collection none, no tracking, no account, notes + transparency counts in Mono, link to /transparency/#allpaid, privacy policy and support links
  14. Questions: faq as ruled details rows
  15. Switching from: alternatives_to (4 linked pages, Truebill and Chronicle Bills as text) + related_journal
  16. Quick reference <details> (ai-canonical), visible
  17. More from Lagerland: you-might-like (computed)
  18. Closing Notes box (badge, QR, price) + imprint line 'Built by Lagerland Apps · updated 13 May 2026 · first released 1 Jan 2026', then the Lagerland strip

Navigation

A planner header bar with 'AllPaid' and five text links (The year · The key · Prices · Compare · Questions) in Next 700 16px. With JS, a 10px navy dot before a link marks the current section (scroll-spy); without JS the links are plain. On mobile, 'Menu' opens a white sheet with the same links in a ruled list.

Motion

Stickers stick: a dot scales 0.85→1 in 90ms with no bounce. Cascades run top to bottom at 30ms per month. The marker ring draws once (stroke-dashoffset, 400ms) when the grid enters the viewport. Everything else holds still. prefers-reduced-motion: no scale, no draw, no cascade.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Alternatives pages are the planner's printed back page: white laminate, one navy header rule, the page's existing H1 (e.g. 'A Rocket Money alternative that doesn't want your bank login') in Next 800 48px, a 68ch reading column in Next 400 18px/1.6, comparisons as ruled grids, and a single strip of the 27th column as the only graphic. Privacy: 'Planner notes — privacy', with the transparency facts as Mono rows. Support: the Notes box enlarged with email, response time and what to include.

Materials

Flat white laminate sheet, no gloss effect · Grid printed in one ink: navy at 25% for cell rules, 100% for month labels, weekend columns tinted · Round dot stickers (14px in cells, 22px in the key) in four category colours with an ink ring · Blank white dots for bills typed by hand (not in the catalog) · Dry-erase marker ring: an irregular 3px navy SVG stroke circling the densest day · Ruled 'Notes' panels in the planner's lower printed area

Colour strategy

Full palette · light

Type rationale

The Braille Institute drew Atkinson so that characters, especially 1/l/I and 0/O, stay unambiguous for low-vision readers. A wall planner is read from across the room and its content is dates and amounts. The Mono sibling aligns the axis and money columns. Three latin files, about 75 KB.

SECOND ROLL

Security Tint Envelope

The security tint printed inside bill and bank envelopes (dense lattices, wave lines and repeated microtext so nobody can read a statement through the paper), together with the windowed business envelope: glassine address window, return-address corner, and the 'POSTAGE PAID' permit-indicia box.

Privacy is the envelope, not a shield icon. The page is the patterned inside of a bill envelope, and only what you typed shows through the window. It refuses trust-badge rows and 'bank-level security' claims.

  • #0E1930
  • #1A2944
  • #F4F6FA
  • #E4E9F2
  • #A9B5CB
  • #F27B88
  • #3B1730
Type
Libre Franklin 800/600: the window headline at 64px desktop / 40px mobile (800), return address and indicia caps (600) with Libre Franklin 400: the letter and reading columns at 18px/1.6, Courier Prime 400/700: only real data, i.e. statement lines, amounts, due dates, daily totals, transparency counts
Light
Evening at the hall table, opening the post under one ceiling light: the inside of the envelope is shadowed and patterned and the paper is bright. Single dark scheme (color-scheme: dark) with paper windows.
Signature
'Hold it up to the light'. A toggle button (aria-pressed, label 'Hold up to the light') sits beside a second window. Default state, 'With AllPaid': the tint is opaque around the window and only the six sample bills show. Pressed, 'With a bank login': the lattice opacity drops to near zero across the panel and a dense illustrative feed of every transaction appears as redacted rows with generic labels ('Card payment', 'Salary', 'Pharmacy', 'Transfer', amounts blocked out). Its caption reads 'Illustrative: a bank login gives an aggregator read access to every transaction, far beyond your bills' (from the founder story and journal). Technique: a --tint-opacity custom property transition and a class toggle, about 20 lines of JS. No-JS: both states render as two labelled panels, 'What a bank-linked app can read' and 'What AllPaid holds', side by side on desktop and stacked on mobile. Reduced motion: an instant swap.
Remembered as
The page that looked like the inside of a bill envelope: the price where the postage-paid box goes, the app's name in the address window, and a button that held it up to the light to show what a bank login would expose.
Risk
Dark navy with one coral accent sits near the 'near-black + one accent' AI trope; the tint pattern and paper windows must carry it, never a glow. The pattern must stay at about 1.2:1 behind text. The light toggle's transaction feed must stay generic and labelled so it can't read as a claim about a named competitor. The navy echoes the app's own screenshots, so screenshots blend into the ground rather than standing out.

Navigation

The return-address corner is the brand ('Lagerland Apps · AllPaid'), followed by text links set like the envelope's printed endorsement line: Statement · Catalog · Prices · Compare · Questions, in Franklin 600 15px pale, underlined on hover/focus with a coral focus ring. On mobile, 'Menu' opens a paper panel styled as a window with the same links.

Motion

Light changes; paper barely moves. The tint fades over 300ms on the light toggle. The window and enclosures fade up 8px over 200ms once, under html.js. The sticky window slides up in 180ms. The postmark does not spin. prefers-reduced-motion: state changes swap instantly, no translate.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Alternatives pages are the opened envelope: a 160px navy tint band at the top with a small window holding the H1 (Franklin 800 40px), then the reading column on paper #F4F6FA in Franklin 400 18px/1.6 navy, 68ch. Comparison tables use paper rules, with Courier Prime only for prices, and the quick_answer is the first paragraph on a 1px-ruled slip. Privacy: the window reads 'Privacy policy — AllPaid', the policy is set as a letter on paper, and the transparency counts appear in Courier Prime linking /transparency/#allpaid. Support: the return address becomes the contact block (email, response time, what to include).

Materials

Security-tint lattice plus aria-hidden microtext rows ('NO BANK LOGIN · NO ACCOUNT · NOTHING LEAVES THE PHONE' at 6px) as inline SVG patterns over the navy · Glassine window: a rounded paper rectangle with a 2px pale rim and an inner 1px rim offset 3px, no blur · Permit-indicia box: a 1.5px pale ruled rectangle with Franklin caps · Enclosures in different real proportions (statement sheet, DL slip, tri-fold leaflet with crease lines at thirds) · Postmark ring carrying the freshness dates · Courier Prime data lines on paper

Colour strategy

Restrained · dark

Type rationale

Franklin Gothic is the face of American business mail, utility bills and permit indicia, so the envelope speaks its native type. Courier Prime is the laser-printed statement line, kept to data. Five latin files, about 115 KB.

New assets needed

None required: the lattice and microtext are inline SVG patterns. Optional later production task: three hand-tuned security-tint SVG tiles (lattice, wave, microtext).

RightSplit

/apps/rightsplit/ + its privacy and support pages + 5 comparison pages

What the page must prove: In the first viewport: (1) one real-looking bill turning into different per-person totals with tip spread in proportion. This uses the journal's worked example, labelled illustrative: on a $154.65 check the $58 ribeye pays $74.75 and the $14 salad pays $18.04, against $38.66 each split evenly. (2) The promise 'scan, split, send — only you need the app, no account, the receipt never leaves the phone'. (3) The honest price line from price.value: 'Free — Pro from $3.99/yr or $7.99 lifetime'. The default page this refuses: Blue fintech friendliness: white-to-blue gradient, rounded sans, split hero with a phone mockup, cartoon friends or circled avatars, a pie chart, 'Split bills with friends easily', teal-green money accents (Splitwise), a row of feature cards and star testimonials. THE ROLL

Weighed and Priced

Labels printed by price-computing deli and butcher-counter scales (Bizerba, Mettler Toledo, DIGI, Avery Berkel) under the EU unit-price rule (Directive 98/6/EC), which puts a price per kilo beside every total. They are die-cut self-adhesive labels issued one after another on a backing liner. Each has pre-printed spot-colour boxes overprinted in thermal black, small caps field captions (NET WT · PRICE/kg · PRICE), the total in heavy numerals, packed-on and use-by dates, and an EAN-13 with the price embedded (GS1 prefixes 20–29).

A fair split is one rate applied to different weights. The page prints each diner a deli price label: their items are the net weight, the table's tax-plus-tip rate is the unit price (pre-printed cyan and identical on every label), and their total is the price. It refuses the blue-fintech split hero, the avatar pie and the equal-wedge diagram.

Type
Pathway Extreme variable (@fontsource-variable/pathway-extreme, wdth+wght latin file ≈58 KB) at wdth 75 for prices and H1. H1: wght 880 at 112px desktop / 54px mobile. Label prices: wght 900 at 48–72px. Product lines: wght 700 at 22px. Field captions: wght 700 at 11–12px caps, +0.06em tracking. with Pathway Extreme at wdth 100, wght 400 and 600, from the same file: paragraphs at 18px/1.55 (quick answer, how-it-works detail, plateau rule, FAQ, privacy) and ingredient small print at 15px. tnum on every amount, rate and date., none: no mono. Barcode digits and dates use Pathway Extreme tnum.
Light
A shopper reads a label at the counter under flat white shop light, or on a phone in daylight. Everything is printed, matte and bright, so the scheme is light only (color-scheme: light).
Signature
'Reprint the labels'. One label holds the sample receipt (Ribeye 58.00, Pasta, beer 28.00, Burger 20.00, Salad 14.00; tagged illustrative) with a person select on each line, a tax field (8.875%) and a tip stepper (0–25%). Any change reprints the four diner labels. The cyan RATE box takes the same new value on every label. NET and PRICE recalculate using the plateau_disclosure rule (proportional tax and tip, fair-rounding pass), and each EAN-13 is redrawn for the new price. An aria-live='polite' line reads, for example, 'Rate is now × 1.30875 for everyone. Alex pays $18.32.' An unassigned line adds a red 'Not assigned: $20.00' row, the app's own state. No JS: the four labels are server-rendered with the worked-example values and the controls are left out. Reduced motion: labels change in place.
Remembered as
The cyan page of white price labels: every diner's label had the same cyan '× 1.28875' box and a different price. The salad paid $18.04, the ribeye $74.75.
Risk
The metaphor needs one sentence to land (dinner is not sold by the kilo), so the RATE caption must say 'tax + tip ÷ subtotal, the same for everyone' wherever it appears. At a glance, a cyan-and-white page can be mistaken for blue fintech; only the label grammar (black band, captions, heavy prices, barcodes) prevents that. The demo maths must match the app's fair-rounding exactly: rounded naively, the worked example sums to $154.66 against a $154.65 receipt.

App Store route

Badge: the official black artwork appears only on white stock, in a field captioned GET IT (54px desktop, 48px mobile), never on cyan. QR: in the hero label's CODE field on ≥1024px, the spot where a label carries its barcode, and again on the closing label. Page sequence

  1. Hero label: H1, hero.secondary, subheadline in the PRODUCT field; the illustrative four-diner multi-line label (NET · RATE · PRICE); PRICE (price.value); GET IT (badge); CODE (QR); PACKED (release.first_release / last_updated, maker)
  2. WHAT IT IS label: quick_answer as the label's description (speakable), with a FREE FROM line: ads, accounts, tracking, third-party SDKs (0) → /transparency/#rightsplit
  3. Reprint the labels (signature): the interactive sample receipt, tip field and four diner labels
  4. How it weighs: how_it_works intro + 4 steps (Scan · Assign · Tip · Send) as four small labels issued left to right, numbered because the order is real (HowTo)
  5. Calculation method: plateau_disclosure (rule, what_it_does_not_do, 3 notes) printed as the back-of-label small print panel at 18px, 68ch
  6. Price labels: plans as three labels of different widths — Free ($0 forever), Pro · yearly ($3.99 / year), Pro · lifetime ($7.99 once, with its front-matter 'Most chosen' line). Each lists its features as INGREDIENTS; plans_footnote as liner print
  7. On the scale: the 4 screenshots in the CSS iPhone bezel, each standing on a white label base carrying its alt text
  8. Contents: value_points (4) and features (5) as one long label with captioned rows
  9. Weighed for / not for: who_for (5) and who_not_for (3) as two columns of one label, keeping the Splitwise pointer
  10. Other counters: comparison_table as a price-comparison strip (4 columns × 8 rows), RightSplit's column on the cyan pre-print, footnote, inline GET IT badge
  11. Reading the receipt: training_vocabulary (4 groups) in one <details> label, collapsed by default; its overline dropped
  12. Storage and handling: privacy (none / no tracking / no account / 4 notes) plus transparency.yml (camera only, data leaves only via the share sheet, analytics none) → /transparency/#rightsplit, privacy policy, support
  13. Questions: faq (16) as <details> rows on one long label
  14. Other counters nearby: alternatives_to → /alternatives/splitwise/, /tricount/, /settle-up/, /tab/, /venmo-split/; related_journal as the 'Worked example' label
  15. Label data: the Quick reference <details> (ai-canonical), visible and crawlable
  16. Also from this maker: you-might-like (computed from site.apps)
  17. Closing label: badge, QR, price, packed-by and freshness line; then the shared Lagerland strip

Navigation

A thin header label at the top of the roll: 'RightSplit' (back to top) and five plain links — The labels, How it weighs, Price, Questions, Privacy — with a 2px black underline on the current section. On phones, 'Menu' opens a full-width white label listing the same links as captioned rows. In-page anchors only; the Lagerland strip at the foot is the only way out.

Motion

Printed and still. Under html.js only: each label enters by sliding 8px down out of an implied printer slot while fading 0→1 over 140ms (40ms stagger, first reveal only); reprinted labels repeat the same slide; the RATE value crossfades over 100ms; the sticky label rises in 160ms ease-out. No parallax, no count-ups (every price is server-rendered), no hover lifts. prefers-reduced-motion turns all of it off.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

The same roll, quieter. The cyan liner becomes a 24px frame and the gaps; the reading column is one long white label at 68ch, Pathway Extreme 400 (wdth 100) at 18px/1.6. The black band names the page ('PRIVACY POLICY · RIGHTSPLIT', 'SUPPORT · RIGHTSPLIT', 'SPLITWISE ALTERNATIVE'). The H1 sits in the PRODUCT field at 56px (wdth 75, wght 860), and the quick answer is the WHAT IT IS field. Privacy sections become captioned fields (OVERVIEW, DATA COLLECTION, STORAGE, THIRD PARTIES, CHILDREN, CHANGES, CONTACT), with transparency.yml as a FREE FROM line. Support is a contact label with the email and 'what to include' as captioned fields, faq rows below. Alternatives pages set RightSplit and the competitor as two side-by-side labels with the same captions (Workflow, Item-level, Account, Ongoing balances). RightSplit's column carries the cyan pre-print; pick-if lists and a GET IT field close the page.

Materials

Process-cyan backing liner, edge to edge, carrying every label in one vertical run · Die-cut white labels with 10px corners and a 20px liner gap between them, flat (no shadows) · Black registration bars (12×4px) on the liner's left edge at every label gap · Field grid inside each label: 1px black frames with caps captions at the top-left of each field (ITEMS · NET · RATE · PRICE · PACKED · GET IT · CODE) · A pre-printed cyan RATE box on every label, overprinted in black: the colour stays the same, the black data changes · Inline-SVG EAN-13 barcodes that really encode each diner's total (prefix 2), and the App Store QR set in the CODE field where a label's barcode goes · A black band across the top of each label with white reversed caps · An INGREDIENTS / FREE FROM small-print block

Colour strategy

Committed · light

Type rationale

A scale printer sets a label in one grotesk at several widths: narrow and heavy for the price, normal for the product text. Pathway Extreme's width axis (75–100) and weight axis (100–900) do that from one ≈58 KB file. It ships tnum, so $74.75 and × 1.28875 line up down the PRICE and RATE columns. At wght 900 its plain gothic numerals look like a price ticket, not a poster face.

New assets needed

None new: icon, 4 screenshots, assets/qr/rightsplit.svg. EAN-13 barcodes are inline SVG computed from each price (hand-built for the four static labels, regenerated by JS in the interaction).

IMPECCABLE’S PICK

Torn Per Person

The 80 mm thermal restaurant check from an Epson TM-T88-class POS printer: merchant header in double-width capitals, a SERVER / TABLE / GUESTS line, item lines with right-aligned prices and dotted leaders, the suggested-gratuity block US checks print, and the sawtooth edge from the printer's tear bar. At the table it gets marked up with a four-colour ballpoint (Bic 4 Colours, 1970): circled lines, ticks and initials in blue, red, green and black, the way people split a check by hand.

The page is the check itself: one thermal roll running down the screen, its lines circled in four ballpoint inks to show who ordered what, then torn into one short receipt per person, each ending in its own TOTAL. The bill is the interface. It refuses the fintech phone-mockup hero and the avatar pie.

  • #1D1F21
  • #5B5F63

Type
Azeret Mono 700 (latin ≈10.6 KB) for printed headers. The H1 is 'double-height' at 52px desktop / 30px mobile, uppercase via CSS so the source text stays as written. The wordmark, section headers and every TOTAL line are 'double-width' (transform: scaleX(2) on short single lines; wrapping is computable from the fixed 0.6em advance). with Golos Text 400 and 600 (≈12 KB each) for all reading prose (subheadline, how-it-works detail, plateau rule, FAQ answers, privacy) at 18px/1.6 in a 64ch column. Azeret Mono 400 for receipt lines and amounts at 17px, with tnum., Nanum Pen Script 400 (≈15 KB) for ballpoint initials, names and margin notes only, at 24px or larger. Never body text, and every handwritten name is also printed.
Light
The check has just landed on the table and someone is reading it on a phone in a bright room. The page is the paper, matte and cool white, with ink on it, so the scheme is light only (color-scheme: light).
Signature
'Tear it'. Under the check sits a printed line, '- - TEAR ALONG THE INK - -', that works as a button. Pressing it pulls the check apart into four narrow receipts: four across at ≥1024px, two by two on mobile. Each receipt is headed by the person's initial in their ink and lists their lines, TAX SHARE, TIP SHARE and a double-width TOTAL (Dana 74.75, Ben 36.09, Cara 25.78, Alex 18.04). A fifth strip in faded grey reads 'SPLIT EVENLY: 38.66 EACH'. Before tearing, tapping a line on the check moves it to the next person's ink, and the torn totals recompute with the plateau_disclosure rule. aria-live announces 'Alex: 18.04'. No JS: the four torn receipts are server-rendered under the check with the worked-example values, and the button is absent. Reduced motion: the torn receipts appear in place without separating.
Remembered as
A long white receipt with its lines circled in blue, red and green pen that tore into four little receipts, one per person, each with its own total.
Risk
Familiar: the page-as-receipt is the obvious creative answer for a bill app, and receipt-styled pages are a known web trope (receipt generators, playlist receipts). Its strength has to come from the ink assignment and the tear, not the paper. Long lines of mono tire the eye, so prose must stay in Golos. Handwritten initials must stay legible at 24px and never carry meaning alone.

Navigation

The receipt's header line is the nav: 'RIGHTSPLIT' (top) and five plain links — The check, Tear it, Price, Questions, Privacy — in Azeret 400 with a dotted underline that becomes a solid ballpoint-blue underline on hover and focus. On phones, 'Menu' opens a short paper slip listing the same links as receipt lines with dotted leaders.

Motion

Paper does not glide. Under html.js only: ink circles draw on once (SVG stroke-dashoffset, 320ms each, 80ms apart) when the check enters view; the tear moves the pieces 12px apart in 180ms ease-out; the sticky slip rises in 160ms. No scroll-jacking, no count-ups. prefers-reduced-motion: ink starts fully drawn, tears are static, nothing moves.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

One long receipt at 68ch. Privacy, support and alternatives pages print as a single roll: a double-width header ('PRIVACY POLICY — RIGHTSPLIT'), the quick answer as the message block between '* * *', headings in Azeret 700, reading text in Golos 400 at 18px/1.6. Sections are divided by dotted rules, not tears (tears belong to the app page's per-person split). Ink appears only as the blue link underline and one margin note per page. Alternatives pages set two receipts side by side, 'RIGHTSPLIT' and the competitor, with matching lines (Workflow, Item-level, Account, Ongoing balances), then 'Pick RightSplit if' ticked green and 'Stick with Splitwise if' in black. Support prints the contact block as a receipt with the email on the TOTAL line.

Materials

Thermal paper drenched edge to edge, cool white · Sawtooth tear edges (CSS mask, 10px teeth) at the top and bottom of each receipt piece, with a 24px graphite gap of tabletop between pieces · Dotted leaders (SUBTOTAL ........ 120.00) and '* * *' separators · Double-width and double-height printed headers · Ballpoint marks as inline SVG strokes: circles around assigned lines, ticks, strike-throughs, an arrow into the margin; initials in Nanum Pen Script · Faded thermal grey for secondary print · The app's screenshots in the CSS iPhone bezel, resting on the paper like a phone put down on the check

Colour strategy

Full palette · light

Type rationale

Receipt lines are fixed-pitch data, so a monospace is honest here, not a costume. Azeret Mono's squared grotesk forms sit close to a POS printer's built-in font, and it has nine weights and tnum. Golos Text is a plain, open screen grotesk, so the explanation reads as prose rather than more receipt. Nanum Pen Script is a quick ballpoint hand and the only face that is written rather than printed. ≈60 KB in all.

New assets needed

None new: ink marks are inline SVG paths, the check is set type, and the screenshots, icon and QR exist.

SECOND ROLL

Cards in the Folder

The restaurant check presenter: a padded leatherette book-fold, about 24 × 12 cm closed, with stitched edges, a clear vinyl pocket for the check, a card slot, a small card pocket and a pen loop, and the house name foil-stamped on the cover. It ends every group meal the same way: each diner slides a card into its top edge, so the folder goes back with the cards fanned out above it and the server asks 'split it evenly?'

A meal ends in a folder that arrives once and goes back once. The page is that folder opened on the table, with each person's own amount standing up out of its top edge where the cards go, so the visitor sees four different numbers come back instead of one total cut four ways. It refuses the split hero and the avatar pie by making the folder's two leaves, its pockets and its top edge the page's structure.

Type

Light
A dim dining room late in the evening. The folder lies open on a dark table in front of whoever picked it up; the light is low, the leather matte, and the only bright things are the foil, the cards and one paper card. The scheme is dark only (color-scheme: dark).
Signature
'Split it evenly?' A foil-stamped two-way switch (a real radio group) sits beside the cards: 'By what each ordered' (default) or 'Evenly'. Choosing Evenly lowers or raises all four cards to the same height and changes them to $38.66, and each card gains a thread-colour line with its difference: Alex '+$20.62', Dana '−$36.09'. Switching back restores the RightSplit amounts. aria-live reads 'Evenly: everyone pays $38.66. Alex pays $20.62 more than by item.' No JS: the cards render at by-item heights, with a printed line underneath: 'Split evenly it would be $38.66 each — Alex would pay $20.62 more than the salad cost.' The switch is hidden. Reduced motion: heights and amounts change instantly.
Remembered as
The burgundy leather check folder with four coloured cards sticking out of the top, each a different height and amount, until you pressed 'Evenly' and they all sank to $38.66.
Risk
Dark, warm leather sits near the steakhouse rendition, so it must stay off gold, scripts and serifs. The folder must remain one folder: two leaves on desktop and one on mobile, with no extra flaps. Its sections below the hero are stitched compartments of the same leather, so the object reading can thin into 'dark page with dashed borders' if the stitching is not drawn with care. Card shapes could imply that RightSplit takes payment, which it does not, so the copy must say 'RightSplit does the math; everyone pays their own way'. Light-on-dark reading needs the paper card for long text.

Navigation

A quiet row on the table above the folder: 'RightSplit' (top) and five links — The split, How it works, Price, Privacy, Questions — in Onest 500 thread colour, turning foil with a cyan underline on hover and focus. On phones, 'Menu' opens a stitched leather panel listing the same links as foil-stamped lines. The Lagerland strip below the back cover is the only way out.

Motion

Leather does not move; cards do. Under html.js only: the four cards slide up out of the pocket on first reveal (translateY 40px→0, 240ms ease-out, 60ms stagger); the switch changes card heights over 200ms ease-in-out; the sticky strip rises in 180ms. No parallax, no glows, no count-ups. prefers-reduced-motion: cards are already standing, heights change instantly.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

The folder closed. Privacy, support and alternatives pages show a single oxblood leaf with stitched edges and a foil-stamped title ('Privacy policy', 'Support', 'RightSplit vs Splitwise'). The reading column is the paper card held in the clear pocket: foil-white #F3E8EA ground, table-ink text, Onest 400 at 18px/1.65, 66ch, headings in Funnel 600. The quick answer is the first foil-stamped panel on the leather above the card. The transparency.yml facts are blind-stamped beside the privacy text. Alternatives pages stand two cards out of the top edge, 'RightSplit' (cyan) and the competitor (foil white), and print the comparison as two columns on the paper card, with pick-if lists and the badge in a slot at the foot.

Materials

Oxblood leatherette across the page, with a faint inline-SVG feTurbulence grain at 4% opacity (vector, no raster) · 1px dashed thread seams stitched 14px inside every edge of the folder and between compartments · Foil-stamped type: flat white foil with a 1px darker inner offset for the stamp edge, no gradients · Blind-stamped lines, tone-on-tone in thread colour, for maker and freshness · Clear vinyl pocket: a flat 6% white overlay with a 1px highlight on its top edge, no blur · A card slot (a stitched horizontal slit) and a small card pocket · Matte flat cards in cyan, mint, lilac and foil white, with 10px corners · The spine: a 2px darker crease down the middle of the open folder on desktop

Colour strategy

Drenched · dark

Type rationale

Hot-foil stamping fills in fine joins. Funnel Display's notched joins (visible in n, k and a at display sizes) look like a die cut to survive that, and it stays crisp at 80px on dark leather without the gold-script steakhouse cliché. Onest has open apertures and a generous x-height, which hold up as light text on a dark ground. ≈52 KB in all.

New assets needed

None new: grain and stitching are CSS and inline SVG, and the cards are set type. Optional later: Apple's official white 'Download on the App Store' badge artwork, if the owner wants the badge directly on leather instead of on a foil-white tab.

THE ROLL

Held Over

The changeable-letter marquee of a neighbourhood single-screen cinema. Its parts: a backlit translucent attraction board with horizontal letter tracks; black and coloured slotted letters hung by hand each day with a pole (zip-change letters, US, from the 1930s); chaser-bulb borders; a structural-glass fascia; lit poster cases along the entrance; a box office with a speaking grille and a ticket tray. Its vocabulary: NOW SHOWING, TODAY ONLY, HELD OVER (a run kept on because it is still going), COMING TOMORROW, ADMISSION, running time.

Today is the only feature on the bill. The page is a cinema front whose attraction board carries the day's showtimes, and anything unfinished is HELD OVER to tomorrow in the marquee's own words. It refuses the split hero and the feature-card grid in favour of a working letter board, a box office and an arcade of lit cases.

Type

Cabin 500 for nav, labels, plan names and captions., Big Shoulders Display 600 with tabular figures for showtimes, prices and running time (real data). No mono.
Light
Someone on the pavement at blue hour, phone in hand, deciding what tomorrow holds under a neighbourhood cinema's lit attraction board, the brightest thing on the street. Dark scheme (color-scheme: dark): blue-hour fascia as the ground, lit white panels as every reading surface.
Signature
'Close today's show': a real <button aria-pressed> on the showtimes board. When pressed, the three finished showings' tiles unhook and drop off the track letter by letter (translateY plus a 6° swing, 18ms stagger). CALL DENTIST 20.15 slides down to the HELD OVER track, and its date tiles re-hang from MON 26 to TUE 27. Pressing 'Reopen Monday' reverses it. Each board has a visually hidden plain-text twin, and the tiles are aria-hidden. No-JS: the board is server-rendered in its final honest state, with the three finished showings in grey 'shown' letters and the HELD OVER track already reading CALL DENTIST 20.15 → TUE 27. Reduced motion: an instant swap with no drop or swing.
Remembered as
The planner whose site was a lit cinema marquee: the unfinished dentist call wasn't a failure, it was 'HELD OVER' to Tuesday, and the App Store badge sat in the box-office ticket tray.
Risk
This is the lowest-resonance candidate on my list: a cinema is nobody's planner. If bulbs and tiles spread beyond the two boards, the price board and the sticky strip, it will read as theme-park kitsch. The night scene sits next to the 'dark + glowing edges' rut, so there is no blur glow and the bulbs stay flat dots. Tiles read worse than set type, so each board stays at or under 40 characters and every tile string has a plain-text twin. Planning is a morning act; a marquee is an evening one.

Navigation

The nav band carries the brand and links. 'TASKFUL DAY' (icon + name) sits at left and links to the top. Five in-page links in Cabin 500 sit on the fascia at right: Showtimes, Running order, Admission, Questions, Box office (→ #get). A single amber bulb dot before a link marks the current section (aria-current). On mobile, 'Programme' opens a lit panel with the same anchors plus Privacy and Support. The nav does not stick; the mini-marquee download bar is the only sticky element.

Motion

Letters hang rather than fly. When the attraction board and the showtimes board first enter view, their tiles settle onto the tracks with a 2° swing that damps out in 380ms (transform-origin top centre, 14ms per letter); no other region animates on load. The bulbs never chase continuously: a single 700ms chase pass runs around the box office when the badge receives hover or focus. Everything else holds still. With prefers-reduced-motion there is no swing and no chase, and tiles render in place.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Privacy and support: the canopy shrinks to one lit track under the nav band, reading 'TASKFUL DAY · PRIVACY POLICY' or 'TASKFUL DAY · SUPPORT' in 28px tiles. Below it, a single lit reading panel (#F4F6F8, Cabin 400 18px/1.65, 66ch) sits on the midnight ground. The h2s are Big Shoulders 700 26px set as plain type, not tiles. The privacy page opens with the House rules frame and its transparency figures; the support page puts the developer email in a box-office window. Alternatives pages become a DOUBLE FEATURE board ('TASKFUL DAY / STREAKS' on two tracks), with the page's quick_answer as the programme note, the head-to-head table as a two-column programme listing, 'Pick Taskful Day if… / Stick with Streaks if…' as two notice frames, the FAQ rows, and a closing box office with the badge.

Materials

Lit attraction board: a #F4F6F8 panel with horizontal letter tracks drawn as 1px #9FB0CC rails at a fixed pitch · Zip-change letter tiles: each capital on its own faintly lighter tile with notch tabs top and bottom (CSS pseudo-elements), black or blue only · Midnight structural-glass fascia with a 2px stainless trim line · Chaser-bulb borders: rows of flat 10px amber discs at 24px pitch, no blur glow · Box office: a recessed lit window with a perforated speaking grille (radial-gradient dot grid) and a stainless ticket tray · Poster cases: lit frames with a stainless edge and an engraved title plate, holding screenshots in the CSS iPhone bezel · Notice frames: smaller lit panels for house rules, the price board and the classification card

Colour strategy

Committed · dark

Type rationale

Big Shoulders was drawn for the City of Chicago from its theatre-district and industrial signage. Its tall, flat-sided capitals sit on a tile the way zip-change letters sit on a track, and they stay legible at 18px on a phone. Cabin is a humanist sans modelled on Johnston and Gill, the lettering of interwar cinema fronts, programme leaflets and the transit posters that advertised them, so the reading copy sounds like the cinema's printed programme. About 63 KB in total (2 × 14.5 KB + 2 × 17 KB).

New assets needed

Nothing new is needed to ship. The tiles are CSS plus Big Shoulders, the bulbs and grille are CSS, and the poster cases use the six existing screenshots. Production follow-ups: screenshots of the four named views and of the Mac app, to replace typeset listings with real posters, and corrected alt text for screenshots 2–6.

IMPECCABLE’S PICK

Tomorrow's Card

The ruled 3×5-inch index card (bright white stock, pale blue rules at a quarter inch, one red header rule) and the Ivy Lee method told since 1918: each evening, write tomorrow's most important tasks on a card, work them in order, and carry anything unfinished to the next day's card. Also the binder-clipped card stack Merlin Mann named the 'Hipster PDA' in 2004, and the A–Z guide cards with staggered tabs found in every card file.

One card holds one realistic day. The page is a clipped stack of ruled cards on a desk: today's card on top, and tomorrow's next, with the unfinished line already copied across. It refuses the infinite backlog list, the split hero and the icon-card grid.

Type
Shantell Sans 700 and 500 for the written layer: the H1 at 56px desktop / 34px mobile, card titles at 32px, task lines at 22px, margin dates and arrows. It is never used for paragraphs. with Inclusive Sans 400 and 600 for the printed layer: body at 18px on a 32px line, locked to the card rules, plus tables, FAQ, and prices in tabular figures., None. Times, prices and counts use Inclusive Sans tabular figures.
Light
At the desk beside the Mac in clear morning daylight, writing today's card before the work starts. Light scheme (color-scheme: light): white card stock on a pale ash-grey linoleum desktop.
Signature
'Carry it over': a 'Finish Monday' button sits on the hero card. Pressing it fades the three struck lines to pencil grey and lifts the Call dentist line off rule 4, moving it (FLIP transform) onto rule 1 of Tomorrow's card. Monday's card slides down and tucks behind the stack, and Tuesday's card comes to the top with 'from Mon' beside the carried line. 'Back to Monday' restores the stack. No-JS: both cards stand in sequence, Monday showing the ink arrow '→ Tue' and Tuesday already carrying the line, so the same truth is stated statically. Reduced motion: an instant swap with a 120ms opacity change and no movement.
Remembered as
Their website was one index card per day. Monday's dentist call got an ink arrow and was already written on Tuesday's card underneath, and the App Store badge was printed in the card's corner box.
Risk
Familiar: a notepad or index card is the classic skeuomorph for to-do apps. It only reads as award work if the 32px baseline lock, the true 5:3 hero card and the carry-over interaction are executed exactly; otherwise it is cute stationery. Shantell Sans turns playful if it spreads, so it stays at 500/700 and never sets paragraphs. A 3×5 card cannot hold a long FAQ, so long sections continue on 'cont.' cards rather than stretching the card's form.

Motion

Paper moves slowly and stays flat. Cards slide in 260ms ease-out with at most 0.4° of rotation and no bounce. On first view the three strike-through marks draw left to right (SVG stroke-dashoffset, 280ms each, 120ms apart); this is the only animation on load. Guide tabs rise 4px on hover and focus. Everything else is still. Under prefers-reduced-motion the strikes render already drawn and cards never move.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Privacy, support and alternatives pages are a single long card on the desk, with the binder clip and guide tabs (Back to Taskful Day, Privacy, Support). The card's title band holds the page title in Shantell 700 40px over the red header rule, and the reading column is Inclusive Sans 18px/32px on the rules at 66ch. Long pages continue onto 'cont.' cards. The support page puts the developer email in the printed box. Alternatives pages set the comparison as a ruled two-column card ('Taskful Day | Streaks'), then put the 'Pick Taskful Day if… / Stick with Streaks if…' lists on a second card, then the FAQ rows, and end with the printed box holding the badge.

Materials

Card stock: flat white rectangles with a 1px #C2C6BF edge and a two-layer soft paper shadow (no hard offset) · Cyan rules at 32px pitch: the global baseline grid, with every line of text sitting on a rule · One red header rule per card, under a 96px title band · Ballpoint ink: strike-through marks on finished lines, the carry arrow '→ Tue', and a hand-drawn SVG loop circling the highlight plan · Binder clip (CSS: a dark steel trapezoid with two wire handles) gripping the stack's top-left corner · Guide cards: staggered tabs rising from the stack's top edge, used as the navigation · Pale ash linoleum desk: a flat matte ground

Colour strategy

Restrained · light

Type rationale

An Ivy Lee card is handwritten, but script fonts are costume and hard to read. Shantell Sans is a marker-hand sans engineered by Arrow Type for legibility, with real forms and spacing, so the plan lines look written on the card at no legibility cost. Inclusive Sans was drawn for readability (distinct I/l/1, open apertures, generous spacing), which suits an audience that includes many ADHD and dyslexic readers. It sits under the hand like the card's own printing. About 120 KB (Shantell 2 × 47 KB + Inclusive 2 × 13 KB).

New assets needed

Nothing new is needed to ship. The cards, rules, clip, tabs and ink diagrams are CSS and inline SVG drawn in code, and the screenshots already exist. Production follow-ups: real screenshots of the four views and of the Mac app, and corrected alt text for screenshots 2–6.

SECOND ROLL

Wound to Twenty-Five

The mechanical 60-minute kitchen dial timer: the tomato-shaped one Francesco Cirillo used as a student in the late 1980s, which named the Pomodoro Technique, and the coloured-body, black-cap dial timers of European kitchens. Its parts: a printed minute scale with long 5-minute ticks turned against a fixed index; a knurled grip; a moulded body in one colour; the bell at zero; the leaflet ('turn past 10, then set'). A timer keeps no record. Every wind starts from nothing.

A timer remembers nothing it could hold against you. The page is one wind-up dial seen from above: set it to 25 and the page itself enters Focus Orbit. The day is the same dial at 24-hour scale, carrying what's left past midnight onto the next turn. It refuses the phone-mockup hero, the feature grid and the tomato.

  • #2A2A26
  • #FCFCFA
  • #17181C
  • #2B5FC6

Type
Rubik 700 for the H1 (72px desktop / 40px mobile) and section heads on the body (40px). Rubik 600 for the dial numerals (18–40px around the scale) and the countdown. with Rubik 400 and 500 for reading copy at 18px/1.6 on the face and on the body. 500 is for labels, nav and plan names., Rubik 600 tabular figures for dial values, the countdown, times and prices (real measurements). No mono.
Light
Morning sun on the desk beside the keyboard, with a sun-yellow wind-up timer under a graphite cap seen from directly above, white dial face up. Light scheme (color-scheme: light), drenched in the body colour.
Signature
'Wind it': the scale ring is a real ARIA slider (role=slider, 5–60 minutes, step 5, default 25), turned by drag, the arrow keys or ± buttons, with the numerals rotating under the fixed index. 'Start' puts the page into Orbit: the yellow ground turns graphite, the reading column narrows to 60ch, and the nav, screenshots and sticky price fade to 20%. The sticky rim shows the countdown (mm:ss, Rubik 600 tabular). At zero the bell line reads 'Session logged. Whatever's left rolls to tomorrow.' Esc or Stop exits, nothing is stored, and focus is never trapped. No-JS: the dial renders set to 25 with the printed line 'Focus Orbit: 25-minute default, configurable', and the slider controls are absent. Reduced motion: the ring snaps between values without spinning, Orbit changes colour instantly, and the countdown digits still update.
Remembered as
A giant sun-yellow kitchen-timer dial with the App Store badge on the knob. Winding it to 25 dimmed the whole site into focus mode, and the unfinished dentist call spiralled past midnight into Tuesday.
Risk
Pomodoro is productivity's most clichéd image, and a timer by itself speaks only for Focus Orbit, one of four views. If the day spiral doesn't carry the rollover, the page sells a timer app. A drenched yellow is loud for a 'calm' brand, so the white face and the graphite cap must take most of the reading. Text inside a circle wastes width, so long copy leaves the circle after the hero. Orbit mode must stay opt-in and fully escapable.

Motion

Mechanical and damped. The ring turns in 220ms ease-out steps of 5 minutes, with no inertia or flinging. The title sits on the yellow in Rubik 700 44px ink, beside a small 25-dial mark. The privacy page opens with the base-label block of transparency figures, and the support page puts the developer email on the knob. Alternatives pages place a two-column comparison on the face ('Taskful Day | Streaks'), then 'Pick Taskful Day if… / Stick with Streaks if…' as two leaflet panels, then the FAQ, and end with the knob holding the badge.

Materials

Moulded body: a flat #F4C443 ground with no gloss and no gradient · Graphite cap and knurled rim: 1px vertical ribs at a 6px pitch (repeating-linear-gradient) on #2A2A26 · Printed dial scale: 60 one-minute ticks, long 5-minute ticks, numerals 0–55 (server-rendered inline SVG, rotated by a CSS custom property) · Fixed index: a blue triangle at the top of the dial that never rotates · Centre knob: a raised white disc with a ring shadow, holding the badge · Instruction leaflet: white folded panels printed in ink and index blue, with numbered steps and small line diagrams · Base label: a white rounded-rectangle sticker printed with maker data

Colour strategy

Drenched · light

Type rationale

Rubik's slightly softened corners read as injection-moulded plastic, the timer's own material. That lets one family speak for the whole object: the numerals printed on the scale, the label on the body and the leaflet text. Its figures stay distinct at 18px set around a dial. About 76 KB (4 × 19 KB).

New assets needed

Nothing new is needed to ship. The dial scale, the day spiral and the leaflet diagrams are inline SVG and CSS drawn in code, and the screenshots already exist. Production follow-ups: real Focus Orbit, Day Clock, Energy River and Day Map screenshots and a Mac screenshot, plus corrected alt text for screenshots 2–6.

Or the category standard, played straight: a white page with an iOS-blue accent; a split hero with the headline and a 'Download Free' badge on the left and an iPhone mockup of the Today screen on the right; a row of four icon cards (Plan / Focus / Everywhere / Private); a pricing table with Pro · Annual highlighted; and an FAQ accordion.

Soon.

/apps/soon/ + its privacy and support pages + 5 comparison pages

What the page must prove: In one viewport: this is not a timer. The countdown is a photo of the actual future plus a plan that writes itself backward from your date (T-30 book flights … T-1 check-in opens), visible on Lock Screen and StandBy. It is free to start, Premium from $1.99/mo or $12.99 once, with no ads, no account and no tracking, and the official App Store badge (plus the QR on desktop) is in reach.

The default page this refuses: The countdown-app landing page: a ticking DD:HH:MM:SS demo timer or confetti numerals over a pastel gradient, a tilted iPhone with stacked widgets, a row of icon feature cards (Widgets · Weather · Checklists · Privacy), three pricing cards with 'Most popular', a star-rating strip and an FAQ accordion. The incumbent adds cream ground, Newsreader and a split hero.

THE ROLL

First Light

The app's own icon (a flat sun breaking a curved dark-teal horizon under a violet → rose → peach sky), read through the almanac's twilight table: the named phases before sunrise (astronomical −18°, nautical −12°, civil −6°, sunrise 0°) as printed in nautical almanacs and sun-altitude tables, and the long northern dawns of the developer's Finland.

The page is one dawn. The visitor scrolls down through flat, hard-edged bands of twilight sky, each band one stage of the run-up (far off → planned → forecast → the day → afterwards), while the real countdown rises over a horizon that carries the download. It refuses the category's ticking DD:HH:MM:SS timer over pastel feature cards.

  • #15122B
  • #55305F
  • #A84A62
  • #F2AE78
  • #E8EEF2
  • #1E3846
  • #FFE9C7
Type
Jost 500 for headlines (92px desktop / 44px mobile, #FFE9C7 on night) and Jost 300 for the T-offset numerals on the Plan Mode horizons (120–160px). A Futura-lineage geometric whose perfect-circle o, 0, 6 and 9 read as sun discs; calm and wide, with none of the serif warmth this subject usually gets. with Literata 400 / 600 for body at 19px/1.6 in a 64ch column (About, FAQ, compare, privacy). A screen-born book face that stays readable on every band from indigo to pale morning., Literata 600 tabular lining figures for T-30, $1.99, 2026 Q4 and the sun altitudes (−12°). No monospace.
Light
Someone awake before an early departure, phone at low brightness in a dark bedroom while the window turns from indigo to rose → a fixed dark-to-light ramp: night at the top, morning at the foot.
Signature
Sunrise on scroll. As each band enters, the sun disc on the sticky earth bar and the altitude-scale marker climb from −18° to +6°: IntersectionObserver sets --alt on <html> and CSS translates the disc, using animation-timeline: scroll() where supported. No-JS: the bands, horizon and half-set hero sun render statically, the sticky bar is absent, and badges sit in the hero, on the sunrise band and on the closing strip. Reduced motion: the disc jumps between the five band positions with no tween, and the hero phone sits at its final height.
Remembered as
The countdown site where you scroll from night into sunrise: the phone with the Tokyo countdown was rising out of the horizon, and the download button stood on the ground.
Risk
This is the literal reading of the name and icon, the obvious 'sunrise app' move, and done loosely it becomes a sunset-gradient wallpaper; the hard band steps and the almanac altitudes are what keep it from that. The drenched bands need per-band contrast tuning (the civil rose is the tightest at 5.5:1 with white). A dark top for an app with a light UI means the screenshots glow on indigo and must not be dimmed. The scroll-linked sun is an enhancement only and must fall back to band-step jumps if it janks on low-end phones. Sibling watch: AfterShift (sleep after night shifts) may reach for night/dawn skies, and if it does, this style keeps the curved horizon and the phase bands as its distinguishing system.
Full style card

App Store route

Badge: Apple's black badge (grey keyline, unaltered) stands on the earth, so the download sits on the horizon. It repeats on the sunrise band beside the plans and on the closing strip. QR: desktop ≥1024px only, black-on-white inside its own quiet zone on a #FFE9C7 sun tile, in the hero and on the sunrise band. Sticky bar: once the hero badge leaves the viewport, a 64px earth band (#1E3846) with the horizon's curved top edge docks at the bottom, holding the icon (32px), 'Soon. — Free · Premium from $1.99/mo' and the badge. A small sun disc on the bar's curve climbs as the visitor nears the sunrise band. Price statement: price.value verbatim on the earth, and the full plans ledger on the sunrise band. Page sequence

  1. Night band, hero: wordmark + pre_headline, the headline, the rising screenshot-1 phone over the horizon, and badge + price + QR on the earth
  2. Night band (earth ground): the Quick Answer as a set paragraph (speakable), then the trust line 'iOS · 0 third-party SDKs · no ads · no account · events stay on your iPhone'
  3. Night band, About (#about): show_body under the about_heading H2 in a 64ch Literata column; the four value_points as bold run-in heads within the prose rhythm; one testimonial set large between paragraphs ('Make the waiting itself pretty' — M.B., Reddit)
  4. Nautical band (#how-it-works), Plan Mode: the how_it_works intro and 6 numbered steps (a real sequence) down the left, beside one horizon line ticked T-90 → T-0
  5. Nautical band (#templates): the six Plan Mode templates, each drawn as its own horizon line with tasks hanging as ticks at their true T-offset (pregnancy in weeks) and T-0 at the right where a small sun rises. Without JS all six print stacked; with JS a type switcher plus a 'Your date' field writes calendar dates under each tick
  6. Civil band (#features): 'When the forecast becomes meaningful', with weather from T-10 (Premium, WeatherKit, place name only) and daily notes T-7 → T-0 as two short statements. Then the 7 screenshots stand on one horizon line in a snap-scroll row, each captioned by its matching feature (photo countdowns, Plan Mode, weather, natural-language search, widgets); Memories and Calendar sync appear as text features
  7. Civil band, widgets: Home Screen / Lock Screen / StandBy and the six styles (small, medium, large, ring, minimal, timeline) beside screenshot 6
  8. Sunrise band: who it's for / who it isn't as two plain lists (5 and 3). Then the plans as a four-row ledger (Free, Premium Monthly, Premium Annual marked by the sun disc as the highlight, Lifetime) with prices in tabular figures, the plans_footnote, badge + QR
  9. Morning band: the founder note 'Rebuilt from TheWait — by the person who shipped it.' with bio, the 4 signals, the response-time line and a mailto
  10. Morning band (#compare-heading-soon): the comparison table (Soon. vs Days Matter / Countdowns (Apalon) / Wedding Happy, 10 rows, Soon. column on a pale apricot wash), footnote, inline badge
  11. Morning band, Memories return: a short statement that the event becomes a memory and comes back each anniversary, with the band's small sun completing its arc
  12. Morning band, roadmap: Shipped / Targeted 2026 Q4 / Targeted 2027 H1 / Under consideration, ordered by sun height (shipped = risen), with the disclaimer
  13. Morning band: FAQ (14 details), the Quick reference ai-canonical <details> (always in the DOM), the privacy summary (5 notes plus transparency facts: 0 SDKs, only the coarse destination to WeatherKit) linking /transparency/, the privacy policy and support
  14. Morning band: related journal (Plan Mode post), alternatives_to links, other Lagerland apps (computed), the maker/freshness line (Built by Lagerland Apps · first released 2026-01-01 · last updated 2026-04-13), then a slim sunrise closing strip with badge + QR
  15. The shared 'A Lagerland app' footer strip

Navigation

Desktop: an altitude scale fixed to the right edge. It is a 1px vertical rule with five ticks labelled Night, Plan Mode −12°, Widgets −6°, Price 0° and Questions +6° (Literata 14px). Each tick is an anchor link, and the current band's tick carries a 10px sun disc. The top bar holds the 'Soon.' wordmark (back to top) and a 'Download' text link to the hero badge. Mobile: a 'Contents' button opens a <details> sheet listing the same five bands. Focus: a 2px #FFE9C7 ring on dark bands and a 2px #1B1530 ring on light bands, 3px offset, links in DOM order.

Motion

Slow and vertical only: things rise, and nothing slides sideways or bounces. The hero phone rises 40px over 900ms ease-out on load. Band seams carry no animation (the colour step is the event). The sun disc moves 600ms ease-in-out between altitudes. Template ticks fade up 12px in T-far → T-0 order at a 60ms stagger. Everything runs under html.js, and all content is visible without JS.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Privacy, support and the five alternatives pages share one frame: a 260px night-band masthead with the star field and the earth arc as its lower edge, and the page title in Jost 500 48px set on the earth (e.g. 'Days Matter alternative'). The reading column then runs on the morning band (#E8EEF2) in Literata 19px/1.65 at 66ch, ink #1B1530. Tables are ruled in #A84A62 hairlines with Soon.'s column on an apricot wash, and FAQs are plain details. Each page closes on a sunrise strip with badge, price and QR. Privacy policy fields (overview, data collection, storage, third parties, children, changes) become H2s, with a small transparency-facts table at the top. Support sets the email and the 'usually within a day' line on the earth band.

Materials

five flat full-width sky bands, hard-edged with no continuous gradient, stepping night → nautical → civil → sunrise → morning · the icon's curved earth horizon as an inline SVG arc (#1E3846), reused as the hero floor, the band seams and the sticky bar's top edge · one flat sun disc (#FFE9C7) with a crisp edge: no glow, no blur · a sparse static star field on the night band only (12–16 one-pixel SVG points) · the real iPhone screenshots in a plain dark bezel, rising from behind the horizon · sun altitudes (−12°, −6°, 0°, +6°) set small in Literata at each band seam's right margin, as data in the margin rather than labels above headings

Colour strategy

Drenched · dark-to-light ramp: one designed sequence that ignores prefers-color-scheme. color-scheme is dark on the night/nautical/civil bands and light from the sunrise band down.

Type rationale

A light geometric display against a drenched sky, with a sturdy reading face so the drench never costs legibility. About 59 KB in total: Jost 300/500 ≈ 19 KB, Literata 400/600 ≈ 40 KB.

New assets needed

None new. Hand-authored inline SVG for the earth arc and star field; existing screenshots 1–7, icon, QR (assets/qr/soon.svg) and the badge include.

IMPECCABLE’S PICK

Admit One

The kept event ticket: gig and theatre tickets, boarding passes, and the stub people keep in a drawer or pin to the fridge. Two-colour print on coloured card, a condensed gothic event name (Alternate Gothic lineage), field labels over values (DATE · DOORS · SEAT), a scan code, a serial number, and a perforated tear-off stub with notched ends.

The page is one ticket for the day you are waiting for: the face (the photo countdown and a timeline of T-times), the perforation, and the stub you keep. The App Store badge, QR and price are printed where a ticket prints its entry code and fare. It refuses the category's pastel timer page and the incumbent's split hero.

  • #F3C6D2
  • #2A1232
  • #1A3FB8
  • #F8DCE3
  • #FFFFFF
Type
League Gothic 400 for the event title / headline (uppercase, 128px desktop / 64px mobile), the fares and the stub's big value (120–180px). It is the open revival of Alternate Gothic No. 1, the condensed gothic of gig tickets and show bills. with Sofia Sans 400 / 700 for body at 18px/1.55 in a 64ch column. Field labels use 700 caps at 12–13px +0.1em: these are the ticket's own DATE / SEAT labels sitting over values, not eyebrows over headings., Sofia Sans 700 tabular figures for prices, the serial (App Store ID 6757280643) and T-times.
Light
Someone at the kitchen counter in daylight on the day the booking confirmation arrives, phone in hand → light, single scheme, on coloured card stock (not white, not cream).
Signature
Print your ticket. The visitor picks an event type and a date (native select + date input). The face reprints: the title becomes the event (e.g. 'WEDDING'), the stub shows the days-to-go in League Gothic blue, and each Plan Mode task fills a field with its real calendar date, computed backward from the chosen date in about 40 lines of vanilla JS. At the page foot the closing stub tears along its perforation (rotates 4°, drops 12px) to reveal 'Kept · comes back every year'. No-JS: the illustrative trip ticket plus all six templates as printed rows, with the stub attached and its text visible. Reduced motion: fields update instantly and the stub stays attached with the same text.
Remembered as
The countdown site that was a pink ticket: the price and the App Store button were on the tear-off stub, and the ticket's times were my trip's to-dos.
Risk
It is familiar: a ticket is an obvious anticipation token, and a pink gig-ticket look may read as concert-specific or gendered for weddings and pregnancy. The two-ink discipline must hold, with no third colour creeping in. It must stay clear of Allpaid's 'Security Tint Envelope', so there is no guilloche, lattice or microtext here, only flat two-colour print. The sticky desktop stub costs 340px of width, so the body must still hold a 64ch reading column at 1280px. The trip template is shown beside a Tokyo screenshot, so the field row must be labelled illustrative.

Four links printed along the ticket's top edge as field values, PLAN · SCREENS · FARES · QUESTIONS (Sofia Sans 700 14px caps, 44px tap targets), plus the 'Soon.' wordmark back to top. Mobile: the wordmark and a 'Menu' text button that opens a details panel printed on pale stub card. Focus: a 3px #1A3FB8 outline at 2px offset on every link, field control and the badge.

Motion

Small and paper-like: fields reprint with a 180ms ink fade, top to bottom. The stub tear is the only rotation on the page (300ms ease-out, once). Link hover underlines in spot blue. No scroll-triggered reveals.

Privacy, support and comparison pages

Privacy, support and alternatives pages print on the same pink card. A short ticket face acts as the masthead: wordmark, page title in League Gothic 72px (e.g. 'DAYS MATTER ALTERNATIVE'), and a field row (UPDATED · date / FOR · Soon.), with the stub carrying badge + fare. The reading column below moves to the pale card (#F8DCE3), Sofia Sans 18px/1.65 at 66ch in ink. Comparison tables are fare tables with Soon.'s column in spot blue, and FAQs are plain details. Privacy policy sections sit under 'Conditions' with their real headings. The support page sets the email as the stub's main field, with the response-time line under it.

Materials

one coloured card stock (#F3C6D2) as the page ground, flat, with no paper-texture images · two-ink print, held strictly: aubergine for everything, app-blue as the spot for numerals, fares and the plan · a perforation: a dotted 3px ink rule with half-circle notches cut into the card's edges (CSS radial-gradient masks) · field-label / value blocks on 2px ink rules (WHEN · PLAN · SCREENS · FARE) as the page's typographic system · the printed art panel: a square-cornered crop of the real Moments screenshot (2) with a 1px ink keyline · the scan code: the real QR on a white quiet-zone tile; a serial line 'No. 6757280643' in spot blue

One poster gothic for what a ticket shouts and one clean humanist for what it says. About 42 KB: League Gothic ≈ 10 KB, Sofia Sans 400/700 ≈ 31 KB.

None new. The art panel and gallery use screenshots 1–7 (a crop of screenshot 2 for the hero); the QR, badge include and icon exist; the perforation and notches are CSS masks.

Soon.Doto

Some days you can't wait for.

Countdowns worth waiting for.

SECOND ROLL

T-Minus Clock

The Kennedy Space Center press-site countdown clock (the original lamp-digit board by the turn basin, 1969–2014), the countdown-milestones table every launch press kit prints (T-time | event), and the painted steel, engraved key legends and GO / NO-GO lamps of launch-control consoles. Chosen because, in Soon.'s own Plan Mode journal post, 'T-minus is the native unit of the app'.

The page is one countdown instrument: a black lamp-digit board that steps through your Plan Mode sequence one T-time at a time, set into a pale console whose sections read as a launch press kit (sequence, monitors, manifest, fact sheet). It refuses both the pastel ticking-timer page and the dark neon dashboard.

  • #D3DAE2
  • #15191F
  • #0F1110
  • #FFB21E
  • #F6F7F8
  • #126236
  • #A32019
Type
Doto 700 for the lamp-grid digits on the board ('T-30', '06') at 240px desktop / 120px mobile, numerals and T-times only, never prose and never under 48px. B612 700 for the headline (64px desktop on one line / 34px mobile), section heads and engraved key legends (caps 14px +0.08em). B612 is the open cockpit-display face Airbus commissioned for instrument legibility. with Public Sans 400 / 600 for body at 18px/1.6, 66ch: the open US-government face, used here for press-kit prose, FAQ and privacy., B612 400 for table heads, the T-time column and status legends (WEATHER · DAILY NOTES · NOTIFY).
Light
A planner at a desk on a weekday lunch break under flat office fluorescent light, laptop open from a search result, running their trip like a launch controller → light console with one black instrument.
Signature
Run the count. The board steps through the chosen template's T-times via EARLIER / LATER keys, arrow keys while focused, or RUN THE COUNT, which advances one milestone every 1.6s and stops at T-0. Lamp digits change with a 120ms bulb fade. The WEATHER lamp lights at T-10 and DAILY NOTES at T-7. At T-0 the task line shows the event and 'becomes a memory', and the monitor bay shows the full countdown card. No-JS: the board shows T-30 'Book flights' and the full milestone table renders below it. Reduced motion: no bulb fade, and RUN THE COUNT steps only on press (no auto-advance).
Remembered as
The countdown site with the big black lamp clock: I pressed 'later' and it counted my trip down T-30, T-14, T-3, and lit the weather lamp at T-10.
Risk
Tone: a launch frame on weddings, pregnancy and birthdays can read as cosplay. It must stay procedural and quiet, with no rockets, flags or space imagery: only the clock, the sequence and the console. The photo, Soon.'s emotional core, is demoted to a monitor bay. Instrument worlds sit near Earnlock's LCD pedometer and may sit near Appmeta Pulse's monitoring dashboard, which is why the board is lamp-grid on black, not 7-segment LCD, and the console is blue-grey, not grey-green. Doto is illegible small, so it is used for numerals only and at 48px or larger.

App Store route
